meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'quite'.

examples.trans: That is quite enough for you.

examples.text: Для настоящей любви этого вполне достаточно.
examples.trans: For true love this is quite enough.

meanings.note: emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Настроение у меня действительно очень хорошее.
examples.trans: My mood really is very good.
This is indeed an important question.

meanings.note: device used to detect something, e.g. lie detector

examples.trans: This is a real lie detector.
This is a real lie detector, Fedya.
The lie detector is turned on.

meanings.note: + infinitive; agrees with the subject: должна (f)
Secondary conversational sense ('owe') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

заходить.gloss: to come in, to drop in

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'ходить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to come in', forming an aspectual pair with 'зайти'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to drop in') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Не стой в дверях, смелее заходи ко мне в кабинет!
examples.trans: Do not stand in the doorway, come on into my office boldly!

examples.text: После работы мы часто заходим выпить кофе в соседний бар.
examples.trans: After work we often drop in to drink coffee at the neighboring bar.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'or', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Common neuter noun meaning 'name' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Let's find out the winner's name.

examples.text: Давайте узнаем имя нашего главного победителя!
examples.trans: Let's find out the name of our grand winner!

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'rat', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
slang for an informant or traitor in an organization

examples.trans: There is a rat in the kitchen.

examples.text: Я должен поймать крысу на кухне.
examples.trans: I must catch the rat in the kitchen.

examples.text: То есть ты хитрая маленькая крыса?
examples.trans: So you are a clever little rat?

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'lie, falsehood' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is a real lie detector, Fedya.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'стоящий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('real, genuine').
Secondary conversational sense ('present, current') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ваня, да пойми ты наконец! Это настоящий успех.
examples.trans: Vanya, understand at last! This is real success.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
+ genitive: 'у нас нет выбора' = we have no choice
Secondary conversational sense ('there isn't') (+ genitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
contrast нигде = nowhere (location)

examples.text: Слушайте, да не нужно вам никуда ехать.
examples.trans: Listen, you don't need to go anywhere.

examples.text: Да никуда я не пряталась! Я контролировала ситуацию.
examples.trans: I wasn't hiding anywhere! I was controlling the situation.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'from' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('of') (тошнит от = sick of) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.en: to answer, to reply, to pick up the phone
meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'вечать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to answer', forming an aspectual pair with 'ответить'.

examples.text: Я вам звоню, а вы не отвечаете!
examples.trans: I call you, and you don't answer!

examples.text: Почему ты не отвечаешь на мои вопросы?
examples.trans: Why aren't you answering my questions?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'звать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to call, summon', paired with 'звать'.

examples.text: Дядя Аркадий всё починит и позовёт.
examples.trans: Uncle Arkady will fix everything and call you.

examples.text: Главное, чтобы она не позвала директора.
examples.trans: The main thing is that she does not call the director.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ймать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to catch', paired with 'ловить'.

examples.text: Ты бандитов поймал! Которые банкомат на Гарибальди ограбили.
examples.trans: You caught bandits! Who robbed the ATM on Garibaldi Street.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'clear'.
Secondary conversational sense ('I see') (as a reply) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm going to be mayor, understood?

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'адиться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to sit down', forming an aspectual pair with 'сесть'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: Sit down and hold the door.

examples.text: Садитесь и держите дверь. Никто не войдёт.
examples.trans: Sit down and hold the door. Nobody will come in.

meanings.note: свободен! = you're dismissed (a boss to an employee)
свободен! = you're dismissed (a boss to an employee)

examples.trans: That's all, Samson, you can go!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: once; что скажешь? = what do you say?
Secondary conversational sense ('tell me / tell us') (polite request) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'neighboring' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.text: В соседнем зале играет тихая музыка.
examples.trans: Quiet music plays in the neighboring hall.

examples.text: За соседним столиком сидели приятные люди.
examples.trans: Pleasant people were sitting at the next table.
To a guest at the next table.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'Wednesday', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('environment, medium') (surrounding environment) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Tell me, is today really Wednesday?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'трах'). Common masculine noun meaning 'fear' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Что смотрите, бандерлоги? Вы совсем страх потеряли?
examples.trans: What are you staring at, you monkeys? Have you lost all fear?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'chair', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Put the chair by the table.

examples.text: А зачем нам бревно? Я вот стулья взял!
examples.trans: And why do we need a log? I brought folding chairs right here!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

meanings.note: 'что я за мэр такой' = what kind of mayor am I
Secondary conversational sense ('? = what's this?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
softens a request: только не сердись = just don't be angry
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'мереть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to die', paired with 'умирать'.

ходить.gloss: to walk, to go (on foot, regularly)

meanings.en: to walk, to go on foot
meanings.note: back and forth or habitually; one trip in one direction: идти

examples.text: Мальчик ходит на костылях. А она ещё и активистка.
examples.trans: The boy walks on crutches. And she's an activist, too.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'well'.
Secondary conversational sense ('good, fine') (as an answer) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Хорошо, Виктор Петрович, я сейчас же всё переделаю заново!
examples.trans: All right, Viktor Petrovich, I will redo everything right now!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'a little'.
чуть не + verb: я чуть не упал = I nearly fell

examples.text: Садись, не бойся. Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: Sit down, don't be afraid. I very nearly let you go myself.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
